Consult Summary:
- 28-year-old woman with new-onset, severe (8/10) left posterior (occipital) throbbing headache beginning yesterday mid-morning, not relieved by a single dose of ibuprofen; clinician advised stronger analgesia, paracetamol, rest and hydration with safety-netting for red flags.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - New headache beginning yesterday mid-morning, localized to left posterior/occipital region.
  - Described as throbbing, built up gradually over a short period, pain severity ~8/10.
  - Took ibuprofen (Nurofen) yesterday without meaningful relief.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Onset: yesterday (mid-morning).
  - Course: persistent since onset; not improved after ibuprofen; slept last night.
  - Expected to settle if responds to recommended medication; advised to recontact if not settled in 1–2 days or if worse.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - No change with lying down, standing, bending over, coughing, or sneezing.
  - Clinician recommended a stronger analgesic (agent not specified) regularly with food and paracetamol as adjunct.
  - Rest and hydration recommended.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Denies nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance, photophobia, phonophobia, tingling, numbness, weakness.
  - Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness.
  - No preceding trauma reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior history of significant headaches (patient: “not really”).
  - No recent blood pressure check recorded.
  - No reported systemic symptoms, focal neurologic deficits, or seizures.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Family history: mother with hypertension and history of migraines.

Medications:
- Current / recent:
  - Ibuprofen (Nurofen) — dose/route/frequency not documented (single dose yesterday).
  - Clinician recommended a “slightly stronger” analgesic instead of ibuprofen — agent and dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Paracetamol recommended as adjunct — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies:
  - Patient reports no drug/food/environmental allergies.

Social History:
- Lives with partner.
- Occupation: designer; currently finding it difficult to perform normal work tasks due to pain but has not missed work.
- Tobacco: denies smoking.
- Alcohol: denies regular alcohol use.
- Recreational drugs: denies use.

Family History:
- Mother: hypertension and migraine history. No other family history recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- No labs or imaging ordered or available.
- No diagnostic testing performed during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Most likely a primary headache disorder, with migraine favored (new unilateral occipital throbbing severe headache; family history of migraine). Secondary causes are considered but currently less likely given absence of red flags and focal signs.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Migraine (high likelihood)
  - Supporting: unilateral, throbbing, severe (8/10); family history of migraine; age/gender consistent.
  - Opposing: absence of typical migrainous features (nausea, photophobia/phonophobia, aura); first-ever headache.
- Cervicogenic headache / tension-type (medium likelihood)
  - Supporting: unilateral posterior/occipital location consistent with cervicogenic/persistent musculoskeletal headache.
  - Opposing: no neck pain or movement-triggered pain described; throbbing quality favors migraine.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) (low likelihood)
  - Supporting: new severe headache with relatively rapid onset.
  - Opposing: patient reports gradual build-up (not classic thunderclap), no LOC, vomiting, neck stiffness, or focal deficits.
- (Conflict noted: none between transcript and DDx.)

Issue 1: Acute severe left occipital headache — likely primary headache (probable migraine)
- Assessment:
  - Probable primary headache, most consistent with migraine given unilateral throbbing severe pain and family history.
- Plan:
  - Start recommended stronger analgesia in place of ibuprofen (agent not specified by clinician) — take regularly with food (prescription/dispensing implied but specific agent/dose not documented).
  - Add paracetamol as an adjunct (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Conservative measures: rest and ensure good hydration.
  - Safety-netting: return/seek urgent care if pain worsens, does not settle within 24–48 hours after starting recommended medication, or if new symptoms develop (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, focal weakness, visual changes, loss of consciousness).
  - Follow-up: contact clinic/GP if symptoms persist or recur; clinician indicated to call back if not settled after trying medication.

Issue 2: Rule out secondary causes (e.g., SAH, CVST, intracranial process) — low current suspicion
- Assessment:
  - Secondary causes considered because of new severe headache; however absence of red flags and normal systemic review lower immediate suspicion.
- Plan:
  - No immediate imaging or ED referral documented at this consult.
  - Urgent evaluation (ED and neuroimaging) recommended if any red flag develops: sudden “thunderclap” onset, rapidly worsening pain, loss of consciousness, new focal neurological signs, persistent vomiting, fever with neck stiffness, or other concerning features.
  - If recurrent or progressive headaches despite treatment, consider earlier imaging/referral (to GP/neurology) per clinician discretion.

Issue 3: Cervicogenic/occipital neuralgia or tension-type features — possible alternative/contributor
- Assessment:
  - Could explain posterior unilateral pain; less likely without neck movement triggers or focal tenderness.
- Plan:
  - If pain persists or recurs, consider GP assessment for musculoskeletal/neck evaluation and referral to physiotherapy or pain management as indicated.
  - Consider headache diary and review for patterns/triggers if recurrent.

General plan items:
- Document medication(s) prescribed/dispensed in chart when available (specific agent, dose, route, frequency missing in transcript).
- Advise patient to recontact if no improvement within 24–48 hours after starting recommended therapy or immediately for red-flag symptoms.
- Consider outpatient follow-up with GP or neurology if headaches recur or fail to respond.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: vital signs and physical exam not recorded; pregnancy status not documented; specific name/dose/route/frequency of the “stronger” analgesic and paracetamol not documented; whether a prescription was actually issued and its details not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none noted (DDx aligns with transcript).
- Transcript quality: clear audio; clinician and patient responses intelligible.
